messages.subject: Cut edges not significant
parts:
I executed an experiment over a dataset with 23.132 and 21 continuous clinical variables to generate a path analysis graph using lavaan, my objective is to infer the relationship between the variables. 

As you can see below my estimate for variables G008, R2B1 and P007 are too small, similar to many others 141 edges, although the p-value is significant (probably by sample size).




Then I think would cut edges with values of estimates below 0,10 for example, but reading about effect size I think there is a better way to stablish this cut of edges.

Is there an specific way to calculate a value to cut these very low estimates in PA/SEM  in lavaan?
Can somebody give me some orientation on how to find a good solution about this (is there a way to establish a cut point in lavaan)?
Thank you

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Cut edges not significant
parts:
Ellias,
  This is not strictly a lavaan question and perhaps not even a SEM question given that you might accomplish your goals at least as well using OLS regression with lm(), unless your model is nonrecursive.

  The first thing that I notice is that your raw estimates equal your standardized estimates.  This suggests that you may be analyzing a correlation matrix.  Unless you include a compensatory set of nonlinear constraints in your model, analyzing a correlation matrix will generally give incorrect inferential statistics.  This happens because the variances on the diagonal are fixed to 1 but the inferential statistics assume that they are free to vary across samples.

  You are essentially engaged in an exercise of decomposing bivariate associations into conditional associations.  At one extreme, you could assume that every estimate exactly equals the population value.  This strategy has the advantage of giving you the optimal estimates of the population values and the disadvantage of giving you a conclusion unlikely to replicate on a new sample.  At the other extreme, you could adopt a rule that is insensitive to the data, such as concluding that all the regression weights are zero.  This would have the disadvantage of offering poor estimates of the population values, but would ensure guaranteed replication across samples.

  You are presumably looking for an intermediate approach that gives you a balance between these two extremes.  Adopting a fixed level of statistical significance offers one such intermediate approach.  It sounds as if you would like to nudge your approach closer to the second extreme, trading off accuracy of estimation for replicability by adopting a more simplified model.  This will mean greater model mispecification (due to simplification, two sides of the same coin).  One thing to consider is that if you apply the procedure iteratively, forcing one regression weight to zero can have an impact on other weights in the equation. 

  By applying one rule in terms of the standardized regression weight to all pairs of variables, your approach essentially assumes that the scales of the variables provide no useful information relevant to your decision about keeping the regression weight.  I am not sure what you meant by 'experiment' but if you meant that you manipulated the independent variables, then their variances reflect the design rather than their natural variability.  So, a standardized conditional association involving an IV that has high natural variability may be more interesting than an equal standardized conditional association with an IV that has low natural variability.  So, adopting a fixed cut point for standardized regression weights may not offer the best strategy when used in combination with an experiment (or quasi-experiment).  There may be additional information that you can use to make judgments about what to keep and what to omit.

  Science involves judgment.  If you remove the judgment about individual weights by applying a mechanical rule, you push the judgment up a level to justifying the choice of rule.  Either way, these judgments will depend upon the context and content of your study.

Keith 
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
